planting.note: Direct sow or plant nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, dry, gravelly or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; creosote bush is among the longest-lived plants on Earth, with some clonal rings estimated at over 10,000 years old, but grows very slowly from seed.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, gravelly soil in full sun; creosote bush is the dominant, defining shrub of the Mojave, Sonoran, and Chihuahuan Deserts, with small, resinous, dark green leaflets that release the sharp, distinctive scent of rain on the desert (petrichor) when wetted, the source of the plant's common name. Small yellow flowers appear after rain in spring, followed by small, round, fuzzy white seed capsules, and the plant can flower opportunistically after any significant rainfall throughout the warm season. It is exceptionally slow-growing but extraordinarily long-lived and drought tolerant, surviving on minimal rainfall by way of an extensive, far-reaching root system that also chemically suppresses competing plants nearby. Give it plenty of room and avoid any supplemental irrigation once established, since regular watering shortens its life and encourages the same root rot that kills most other true desert natives when overwatered.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant nursery starts into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; brittlebush is one of the most common and recognizable low desert shrubs, blanketing hillsides in gold each spring.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; brittlebush is a rounded, silvery-leaved desert shrub whose felted, gray-white foliage reflects intense sun and reduces water loss, and it is one of the most visually dominant plants of the Sonoran Desert, covering hillsides in a haze of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers on tall, leafless stalks each spring. The dried, resinous stems were historically burned as incense by Spanish missions and Native peoples, giving the plant one of its alternate common names, incienso. Fast-growing and short-lived compared to many desert shrubs, it typically declines after five to ten years but self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny, well-drained soil to replace itself. Prune out dead or woody stems in fall to encourage fresh growth, and avoid rich soil or regular irrigation, both of which shorten its already modest lifespan.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; desert marigold is a short-lived, heat-loving reseeding perennial that blooms almost continuously through the hottest, driest part of the desert year.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; desert marigold produces woolly, silver-gray leaves and a nearly continuous succession of bright golden-yellow, papery daisy flowers on slender stalks from spring through fall, thriving in the same intense heat and aridity that stresses or kills most other flowering plants. It is short-lived, generally two to three years, but reseeds itself reliably in loose, undisturbed, well-drained soil, effectively behaving as a self-sustaining perennial population once established. The felted foliage and stems help the plant conserve moisture and reflect intense desert sun, and every part of the plant is mildly toxic if ingested in quantity, so it is not a plant to include in an edible or livestock-accessible planting. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, or let seed heads mature and shatter to maintain a self-renewing colony for years to come.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat lightly and direct sow into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Emory's globemallow blooms opportunistically after rain and can flower nearly year-round in mild desert winters.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; Emory's globemallow is an upright, gray-felted Sonoran Desert native with soft, velvety, three-lobed leaves and abundant, cup-shaped, orange to salmon flowers arranged in loose spikes that appear opportunistically after rain, sometimes flowering multiple times a year in response to seasonal moisture rather than on a strict calendar. It is a fast-growing, short-lived perennial that self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny, well-drained soil, quickly recolonizing bare ground after fire or grading and providing a reliable, low-water source of color and pollinator forage. Fine hairs covering the foliage can be mildly irritating to skin and eyes for sensitive individuals, so handle with care when pruning or clearing spent growth. Cut plants back hard after a bloom flush fades to encourage fresh growth and renewed flowering with the next rain event.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; red justicia tolerates more shade and slightly more regular water than chuparosa, its desert-wash relative in the same family.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; red justicia is a compact, rounded Arizona and Sonoran shrub with small, bright green leaves and clusters of vivid red-orange, tubular flowers produced heavily in spring and again in fall, with lighter, sporadic bloom through summer in favorable conditions. It is a reliable, easy-care hummingbird plant for desert gardens, tolerating both reflected heat in full sun and the dappled light of a partially shaded courtyard or wash-side planting. Established plants are quite drought tolerant, though occasional deep watering during the hottest, driest stretches keeps the foliage fuller and encourages more consistent flowering. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to maintain a dense, rounded form, and expect frost damage to the top growth in a hard freeze, with recovery from the base typical the following spring.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; woolly butterfly bush is far more compact and drought tolerant than the common Buddleja davidii sold widely in nurseries.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; woolly butterfly bush is a compact, rounded Chihuahuan Desert shrub with small, felted, silvery-gray leaves densely covered in soft wool-like hairs, and small, tight, ball-shaped clusters of bright orange flowers in spring and again after summer rains. Unlike the fast-growing, sometimes weedy Buddleja davidii common in nurseries, this species stays naturally compact and slow-growing, making it far better suited to small xeriscape gardens and rock plantings without becoming leggy or invasive. Its dense silvery foliage and modest size pair well with agaves, yuccas, and other true desert plants in a mixed xeriscape border, and it is visited by butterflies and bees during its bloom periods. It requires excellent drainage and minimal water once established, needing only light shaping after flowering to maintain its naturally tidy, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring into very well-drained, dry, alkaline, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Rio Bravo sage blooms most heavily right after summer rain events, functioning as a natural 'barometer bush.'

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, alkaline soil in full sun; Rio Bravo sage is a South Texas native shrub in the cenizo group, with small, silvery-gray, felted leaves and abundant lavender-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers that burst into bloom within a day or two of rain or a sharp rise in humidity, a trait that has earned cenizo shrubs the folk name 'barometer bush' across South Texas. It stays somewhat more compact than the widely planted Texas sage (Leucophyllum frutescens) and tends to flower even more heavily and reliably after rain events. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, it thrives in poor, rocky, or caliche soil that would stress most ornamental shrubs, needing only excellent drainage and full sun. Prune minimally and only to shape, since heavy shearing removes the natural silvery, rounded form and reduces the flush of bloom that follows each rain.
